[MUJAHID:v2p460#2/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | holds | Enslaving the Children of Israel means subjugating them, making them slaves, and putting them to work.
[MUQATIL:26:19-22/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Moses says Pharaoh boasts of his kindness to him alone and forgets his wrongdoing: enslaving the Israelites for the Copts.
[MUQATIL:26:19-22/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | Pharaoh oppressed the Israelites for 430 years, though another report gives forty years more; they were in Egypt when Jacob and his household came to Joseph.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p499/r5] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | Moses's reply refers to Pharaoh's boast about raising him and denies that this was a favor when Pharaoh had enslaved Israel. | mentions 26:19
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p499/r6] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | Moses argues that Pharaoh enslaved his formerly free people, took their wealth, and used their wealth to raise him, so Moses has a stronger claim to it.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p499/r7] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid explains Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel as subjugating, torturing, and exploiting them.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p499/r8] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda paraphrases Moses's rebuttal: Pharaoh boasts of enslaving a free people and subjugating them.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p499/r9] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · ابن مجاهد | reports | Ibn Mujāhid, transmitting his father, glosses the enslavement as subjugation.
[FARRA:v2p279/r4] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Moses concedes that being raised was a favor, while stressing Pharaoh did not enslave him as he enslaved the Children of Israel.
[FARRA:v2p279/r5] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The wording omits “and you left me alone”; that omitted contrast is clear from the example of sparing one servant while beating another.
[FARRA:v2p279/r6] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The clause with an may be nominative as an apposition explaining the favor, or accusative as the favor Moses is reproached for.
[FARRA:v2p279/r7] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Arabs use both ʿabada and aʿbada for enslaving; an unnamed Arab's poem uses yaʿbudunī in this sense.
[MAJAZ:v2p84/r7] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The phrase means that Pharaoh took the Children of Israel as slaves.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p74/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatadah says Moses tells Pharaoh that enslaving the Israelites is the supposed favor Pharaoh holds over him.
[AKHFASH:v2p461/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | وتلك نعمة تمنها علي is treated as a question with أو understood; أن عبدت بني إسرائيل then explains it as a substitute for نعمة.
[TAB-FULL:v17p559#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Moses means Pharaoh's raising him and leaving him unenslaved while enslaving the Israelites; the omitted “and left me” is understood from context.
[TAB-FULL:v17p559#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The phrase “that you enslaved the Children of Israel” can be accusative, tied to Pharaoh's claiming the favor, or nominative, explaining what the favor was.
[TAB-FULL:v17p559#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The verb ʿabbada means to make people slaves; al-Ṭabarī supports this usage with a line of poetry.
[TAB-FULL:v17p559#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | A poem uses the verb ʿabbadanī to mean making someone a slave, supporting al-Ṭabarī's lexical gloss.
[TAB-FULL:v17p559#2/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid explains Pharaoh's enslaving the Israelites as conquering and employing them.
[TAB-FULL:v17p559#2/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj says Pharaoh subdued, overcame, and employed the Israelites.
[TAB-FULL:v17p559#2/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī takes the claimed favor to mean that Pharaoh raised Moses as an infant.
[TAB-FULL:v17p559#2/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | reports | Another reported interpretation makes Moses ask rhetorically whether Pharaoh counts enslaving the Israelites as a favor to him.
[TAB-FULL:v17p562/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda reads Moses's words as a rhetorical question: does Pharaoh claim as a favor that he made the Israelites slaves?
[TAB-FULL:v17p562/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · نحويي البصرة | reports | Some Basran grammarians treat the clause as an implicit question—“Do you claim it as a favor?”—with “that you enslaved the Israelites” appositional to “favor.”
[TAB-FULL:v17p562/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض أهل العربية | reports | Another grammarian rejects that analysis as mistaken: the interrogative hamza cannot be omitted while the clause remains a question; the particle أم is evidence of interrogation.
[TAB-FULL:v17p562/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أكثرهم | reports | Most grammarians take the first clause as a statement and the second as a question, treating أم as equivalent to the interrogative hamza when it follows a clause.
[TAB-FULL:v17p562/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī also cites the objection that a question may omit its initial interrogative hamza when أم follows, illustrating the construction with a poem.
[TAB-FULL:v17p562/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · نحويي الكوفة | reports | The Kufan grammarians adopt al-Ṭabarī's interpretation: Pharaoh's favor was raising Moses, while he enslaved the Israelites and left Moses unenslaved.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p86/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | The commentators read Pharaoh’s words as a reproach, not an acknowledgment of a real favor: how could enslaving the Israelites be a blessing to Moses?
[ZAJJAJ:v4p86/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Although phrased as a statement, the wording rebukes Pharaoh; it implies Moses said the enslavement of the Israelites was a favor because Pharaoh did not enslave him too.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p86/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | عبد الرجل and أعبدته both mean to make someone a slave.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p86/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | One parse makes أن a nominative apposition to نعمة: Pharaoh enslaved the Israelites but left Moses unenslaved.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p86/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Alternatively أن is accusative: Pharaoh’s persecution became a benefit because otherwise Moses’ family would have kept him rather than placing him in the river.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p86/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · الشاعر | reports | The quoted poem uses أعبدني to mean that the people made the speaker their slave.
[IBNABIHATIM:v8p2755#2/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Isḥāq says Moses rejects Pharaoh's supposed favor: Pharaoh enslaved the Israelites and calls that a favor to Moses.
[IBNABIHATIM:v8p2755#2/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says Moses challenges Pharaoh for claiming credit after taking free Israelites and making them slaves by force.
[IBNABIHATIM:v8p2755#2/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid glosses enslaving the Israelites as subjugating them and forcing them into service.
[IBNABIHATIM:v8p2755#2/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Isḥāq says Pharaoh enslaved Israel by seizing their children, enslaving whom he wished and killing whom he wished; Moses was sent to make this known.
[NAHHAS:v3p175/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash suggests an omitted interrogative alif, understanding the wording as a question.
[NAHHAS:v3p175/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | rejects | Al-Nahhas rejects omission of the interrogative alif because it changes meaning; it can be dropped only in poetry when an أم is present, apart from al-Farra's allowance in expressions of doubt.
[NAHHAS:v3p175/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra allows deletion of the interrogative alif in expressions of doubt, as in ترى زيدا منطلقا for أترى; Ali ibn Sulayman attributes this to colloquial speech.
[NAHHAS:v3p175/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra reads Pharaoh's claimed favor ironically: it would be a favor only if he had not enslaved Moses while enslaving the Israelites.
[NAHHAS:v3p175/r18] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak says Moses rebukes Pharaoh for claiming as a favor something he had no right to claim.
[NAHHAS:v3p175/r19] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | The rebuke may also parallel 4:79, which says that misfortune comes from oneself. | mentions 4:79
[NAHHAS:v3p175/r20] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | A fourth analysis supplies an omitted قول; أن عبدت can be nominative as an appositive to نعمة or accusative with the causal sense because you enslaved the Israelites.
[THALABI:v7p161/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan said Pharaoh took the Israelites’ property, spent it on Moses, and made them slaves.
[THALABI:v7p161/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | “You enslaved the Children of Israel” means that Pharaoh took them as slaves; grammatically the phrase can be accusative after an omitted preposition or nominative as an apposition to “favor.”
[THALABI:v7p161/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra read Moses’ words as acknowledging a favor: Pharaoh raised him, did not kill or enslave him as he did Israel’s boys, and left him free.
[THALABI:v7p161/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid read the words as a denial, phrased as a rhetorical question, rather than an acknowledgment of Pharaoh’s favor.
[THALABI:v7p161/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | One explanation of Moses’ denial is that, had Pharaoh not killed Israelite boys, Moses’ own parents would have raised him, so Pharaoh had no favor to claim.
[THALABI:v7p161/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Other explanations are that Moses recalls Pharaoh’s crime against Israel, or argues that enslaving his people cancels any kindness shown to him.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p166/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · علي بن عيسى | reports | ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā says enslaving the Israelites nullified the favor Pharaoh claimed toward Moses.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p166/r12] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ asks how oppressing the Israelites rather than Moses could count as a favor to Moses.

ARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Another view denies Pharaoh had a favor: Moses was raised by Israelites at Pharaoh’s order as part of enslaving them.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p166/r14] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says Pharaoh paid for Moses’s upbringing from Israelite earnings taken through enslavement, so the money was not Pharaoh’s favor.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p166/r15] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · أبان بن تغلب | reports | Abān ibn Taghlib says taʿbīd means confinement and humiliation.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p166/r16] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Taʿbīd can mean enslavement, named for its humiliation, as with a road made trodden; the commentary cites Ṭarafa.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p168/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · طرفة بن العبد | reports | Ṭarafa’s line uses maʿbad for a road made smooth or trodden, illustrating the derivation of taʿbīd from humiliation.
[QUSHAYRI:v2p398/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Pharaoh counted sparing Moses’ life among the Israelites as a favor, but Moses rejects this: enslaving the Israelites is no kindness and gives Pharaoh no claim over him.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن السكيت | reports | Ibn al-Sikkit explains the verbs as making someone a slave and cites Ruʾba's “enslavement” wording; he also says taʿabbada and aʿbada can mean taking someone as a slave.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-Wahidi says these collected explanations do not resolve the verse's difficulty, then frames the main disagreement as whether Moses denies any favor from Pharaoh.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r11] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | The author of al-Naẓm says the phrase must be an incredulous question, understood as “or is that a favor?”, since Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel cannot be a favor to Moses.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r12] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب النظم | reports | The author of al-Naẓm supports an omitted interrogative hamza with Arabic usage and a poetic example meaning “Should I rejoice?”
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r13] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash similarly treats the clause as an incredulous question, with the phrase about enslaving Israel explaining or apposing to “favor.”
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r14] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو العباس | rejects | Abu al-Abbas rejects al-Akhfash's analysis: an interrogative cannot be omitted where it is required, especially when أم still signals a question; he cites the objectionable poetic usage “تروح من الحي أم تبتكر”.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · رؤبة | reports | Ruʾba's line uses taʿbīd for enslavement, as evidence for the wording.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن السكيت | reports | Ibn al-Sikkit says taʿabbadtu fulānan means I took him as a slave, just like ʿabbadtuhu, and that taʾammat means taking a woman as a bondwoman.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | A further cited poetic line uses “you enslave me,” and another uses the form aʿbada for ʿabada; the poets are not named here.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says enslaving the Israelites means subjugating and putting them to work.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · قتادة | reports | Qatada paraphrases Moses as challenging Pharaoh to claim credit for making the Israelites slaves.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says Moses contrasts Pharaoh's claimed favor in raising him with his enslavement of Israel, asking Pharaoh to release them with him and stop tormenting them.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbi reads Moses as saying Pharaoh boasts of favor while enslaving the Israelites.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p36/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Maqatil says Moses acknowledges Pharaoh's alleged kindness to him personally while indicting the enslavement of the Israelites.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p39/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار | reports | Ibn Ishaq reads Moses as denying Pharaoh's alleged favor: Pharaoh enslaved Israel, seized their children, enslaved or killed whom he wished, and thereby caused Moses to be brought to Pharaoh's house.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p39/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj prefers the denial reading: “What favor was enslaving Israel to me?” The declarative wording rebukes Pharaoh, since his killing of Israelite sons forced Moses' mother to put him in the river.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p39/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الأزهري | reports | Al-Azhari explains that if Pharaoh had not enslaved Israel, Moses' family would have raised him rather than casting him into the river; the supposed favor arose from Pharaoh's forbidden oppression.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p39/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The argument works like telling someone who boasts of raising you that he could do so only after killing your parents: naming the cause rebuts the claimed favor.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p39/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المبرد | reports | Al-Mubarrad likewise says Pharaoh raised Moses because of his oppression and attempted domination of Moses' people; grammatically, “that” begins the sentence, “a favor you claim” is its predicate, and “enslaving” explains the favor.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p42/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء، وأبو العباس | reports | Al-Farra and Abu al-Abbas accept that Moses acknowledges Pharaoh's upbringing as a favor: he raised Moses and spared him from the enslavement imposed on Israel.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p42/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra's reading supplies an understood “and left me”: just as a spared servant may call it a favor that another was beaten, Moses contrasts his upbringing with Israel's enslavement.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p42/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra allows أن to be nominative as apposition or accusative after an understood preposition, respectively yielding “your enslaving Israel” or “because you enslaved Israel.”
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p42/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-Wahidi explains that the acceptance reading can be reconstructed with an omitted phrase: “the favor you mention, which you claim because you enslaved Israel.”
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p42/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | prefers | Al-Wahidi says the commentators' explanations show that the denial of Pharaoh's favor is the preferred interpretation.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:26:22-29/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Moses acknowledges Pharaoh's favor in raising him, but says it was a favor only because Pharaoh did not enslave him as he enslaved Israel's children; “enslaved” means made into slaves.
[JISHUMI:v7p5346#2/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | In “an ʿabbadta,” the accusative can remove an implied preposition, meaning by your enslaving or because you enslaved them.
[JISHUMI:v7p5346#2/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Alternatively, the phrase is nominative as an apposition to favor: “the favor of your enslaving.”
[JISHUMI:v7p5346#2/r20] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | One reported interpretation treats Moses' response as acknowledging a favor.
[JISHUMI:v7p5346#2/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Taʿbīd means making a person a slave; the verb has the forms ʿabadtuhu and aʿbadtu-hu.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p110/r10] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Moses may be rebutting Pharaoh for boasting of his upbringing while forgetting his enslavement and mistreatment of the Israelites, whose humiliation also disgraced Moses.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p110/r11] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Another explanation says Pharaoh’s enslavement and killing of Israelite children put Moses in his care; without it, his own family would have raised him and he would not have been cast into the river.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p110/r12] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | ʿAbadta means that Pharaoh made the Israelites into slaves; related forms also mean taking someone as a slave.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p110/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Exegetes differ over Moses’s “that is a favor”: some read it as acknowledgment and others as denial.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p110/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · بعضهم | reports | On the affirmative reading, Moses counts it as a favor that Pharaoh raised him without killing or enslaving him, unlike Israelite boys and people.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p110/r7] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · بعضهم | reports | On the negative reading, “is this a favor?” is a question with the interrogative hamza omitted, as elsewhere in scripture and poetry. | mentions 21:34
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p110/r8] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الشاعر | reports | The poet’s line is cited as an example of the omitted interrogative hamza.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p110/r9] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · عمر بن عبد الله بن أبي ربيعة | reports | ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Rabīʿa’s verses are cited as examples of the omitted interrogative hamza.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p228#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Both readings serve an argument: the first opposes Pharaoh and dismantles his claims; the second makes Moses fair and candid, giving his words greater force against an unfair opponent.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p228/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash proposes an omitted interrogative alif, meaning aw-tilka, but says this works only when paired with am, as in a cited poem.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p228/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | rejects | The author calls al-Akhfash’s analysis forced; Moses’ statement is declarative without an interrogative alif and is sound as Qatāda explained.
